etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English cryme, crime, from Old French crime, crimne, from Latin crīmen. Displaced native Old English firen.

definitions.definition: (countable) A specific act committed in violation of the law.
(countable) Any great sin or wickedness; iniquity.

quote.citation: 1687 (date written), Alexander Pope, “Ode for Musick on St. Cecilia’s Day”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], →OCLC, canto VI, page 376:
quote.text: No crime was thine, if 'tis no crime to love.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto IX”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 46:
quote.text: the tree of life, the crime of our first father's fall

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The habit or practice of committing crimes.
(UK, military, transitive) To subject to disciplinary punishment.

quote.citation: 1846, John Mercier McMullen, Camp and Barrack-room, Or, The British Army as it is, page 298:
quote.text: Nevertheless, in the course of a few days he is again intoxicated, creates disturbance in his quarters, is confined by his sergeant, crimed, and brought before the commanding officer  […]

quote.citation: 1987, Robert Sampson, Yesterday's Faces: From the Dark Side, →ISBN, page 61:
quote.text: If, during the 1920s, the master criminal was a gamester, criming for self expression, during the 1930s he performed in other ways for other purposes.
